title: The King Comes Home
sum: Absalom is dead, and David will not stop weeping. His soldiers creep back into the city as if they had lost. Joab storms in and tells the king the truth: you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. Get up and speak to your men, or by tonight you will have none. David goes and sits in the gate.

Then the long road home begins. The northern tribes argue about bringing David back; David courts his own tribe, Judah, and offers Absalom's general Amasa the command of the army. At the Jordan the people of the revolt come to meet him one by one: Shimei, who cursed him, begs for mercy and gets it; Mephibosheth, lame and unwashed, says his servant lied about him; old Barzillai, who fed the army, declines a place at court. The chapter ends with Israel and Judah quarreling over who owns the king.
readings: Read as a study in mercy and politics

Every meeting at the Jordan is a test of David's judgment. He spares Shimei, splits the land between Mephibosheth and Ziba, rewards Barzillai's son. Some readers see a wise king healing a divided nation; others see a tired man buying peace and storing up grudges for 1 Kings 2.
Read as the start of the split

The chapter's last scene, ten tribes against one, points straight to Sheba's revolt in chapter 20 and to the division of the kingdom after Solomon (1 Kings 12). The return of the king is also the moment the cracks show.

views.H: The return took place late in David's reign, perhaps around 980 BC. The route from Mahanaim to Gilgal and Jerusalem fits the geography of the Jordan valley, and the tension between Judah and the northern tribes is well attested in later history.
views.C: Most critical scholars treat chapters 9–20 as the core of a "Court History" or "Succession Narrative" (Leonhard Rost), a skilled and in places unflattering account of David's family. Some (McCarter, Halpern) read parts of it as political defense of David's actions toward Saul's house.
views.L: Literary readers admire the chapter's pairs: the weeping father and the commanding Joab, the cursing Shimei and the mourning Mephibosheth, the rich Barzillai who asks for nothing and the servant Ziba who gains much. The narrator lets the reader judge each.
views.J: The Talmud sharply criticizes David's verdict on Mephibosheth's land: when David said "you and Ziba will split the land," a heavenly voice said that Rehoboam and Jeroboam would split the kingdom (Bavli Shabbat 56b). The rabbis also count David's eight cries of "my son" as prayers that raised Absalom from Gehenna (Bavli Sotah 10b).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in David's mercy to Shimei a picture of a king who forgives on the day of his triumph, and in Mephibosheth, the lame man at the king's table, a picture of grace to the undeserving. Others warn that the deathbed instructions of 1 Kings 2 complicate any simple reading.

deep.h: Judah and Israel: a kingdom in two parts
deep.b:
From the start David's kingdom was two kingdoms under one king. Judah made him king at Hebron (2:4), and only seven years later did the elders of Israel come to make a covenant with him (5:1–3). Absalom's revolt began in Judah, but it drew in "all Israel." When it collapsed, the north moved first to bring David back, and Judah hung back until David appealed to kinship and offered Amasa the army.

The quarrel at the Jordan (19:41–43) shows how quickly pride and suspicion return. Israel claims ten shares in the king; Judah says the king is its own close kin. The next chapter opens with Sheba's cry, "We have no share in David," and the same cry will end the united kingdom (1 Kings 12:16). The narrator of Samuel does not hide that David's own choices, including his appeal to Judah over the north, made the split more likely.

settings.what: Joab's rebuke of the grieving king
settings.to: King David, in the house at Mahanaim
settings.when: the day of the victory, while the troops slip back in shame
settings.why: Joab tells David he has shamed the men who saved his life. He warns that if he does not go out and speak kindly to them, none will stay by him that night. David obeys and sits in the gate. The rebuke shows that a king's private grief can cost him his kingdom. It also shows the hard power Joab holds over David.

settings.what: David's message to the elders of Judah
settings.by: David, through the priests Zadok and Abiathar
settings.to: the elders of Judah, and Amasa, Absalom's general
settings.when: while the northern tribes are already talking about bringing the king back
settings.why: David asks his own tribe why they are last to bring him home, calls them his flesh and bone, and promises Amasa command of the army in Joab's place. The move wins Judah, but it angers Joab and sets Judah against the northern tribes. Readers see the split that will divide the kingdom after Solomon.

settings.to: King David, at the Jordan crossing
settings.why: Shimei, the man who cursed David, falls before him, admits his sin and points out that he is the first of the house of Joseph to come. David refuses Abishai's call to kill him and swears Shimei will not die. On a day of return, the king shows mercy. Readers later find David telling Solomon to deal with Shimei after his death (1 Kings 2:8–9).

settings.to: King David, on his return to Jerusalem
settings.when: when David asks why he did not leave with him
settings.why: Mephibosheth says Ziba tricked him and lied about him, and points to his unwashed clothes as proof of mourning. David splits the land between them. Readers cannot be sure who told the truth, and many think David could not either. Mephibosheth's answer, that Ziba can take it all, suggests his loyalty was real.

settings.by: Barzillai the Gileadite, a rich man of eighty
settings.when: when David invites him to live at court in Jerusalem
settings.why: Barzillai says he is too old to enjoy the court and wants to die in his own town, and sends Kimham in his place. His words show the gentle loyalty of the people east of the Jordan who fed David in exile, and David repays it. David asks Solomon to keep showing it (1 Kings 2:7).

settings.what: Israel and Judah quarrel over the king
settings.by: the men of Israel and the men of Judah
settings.to: the king and to each other, at Gilgal
settings.when: after Judah escorts the king across the Jordan
settings.why: Israel complains that Judah stole the king; Judah answers that the king is their near kin; Israel says it has ten shares in the king. The argument shows the old divide between north and south, and it leads at once to Sheba's revolt. Readers who knew the later split of the kingdom (1 Kings 12) saw it coming here.

title: No Share in David
sum: The quarrel at the Jordan turns into revolt. Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, blows the ram's horn: "We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse!" The northern tribes follow him; Judah stays with David. Back in Jerusalem David shuts away the ten concubines Absalom had taken, and orders his new commander Amasa to raise Judah's army in three days. Amasa is late.

David sends Abishai with Joab's men instead. At Gibeon Amasa meets them, and Joab greets him with a kiss and kills him with a single stroke. Joab takes back command, chases Sheba to the far northern town of Abel of Beth-maacah, and begins to batter its walls. A wise woman of the town calls out to Joab, reminds him that Abel is "a mother in Israel," and strikes a deal: Sheba's head is thrown over the wall, and the town is spared. The chapter closes with a list of David's officials.
readings: Read as Joab's chapter

Joab is ordered out of command, then murders his replacement and wins the war anyway. The official list at the end puts him back over the whole army as if nothing had happened. The chapter shows how much David depended on a man he could not control.
Read as the wise woman's chapter

The real peacemaker is a woman with no name. She speaks proverbs, appeals to Israel's traditions, and saves a town by giving up one man. With the woman of Tekoa (chapter 14), she shows wise women as respected voices in Israel's towns.

views.H: Sheba's revolt was likely brief and local, but it shows the weakness of David's union of the tribes. Abel of Beth-maacah, now being excavated, was an important town on the northern border.
views.C: Critical scholars see Sheba's revolt as the end of the Absalom story and part of the "Court History." The lists of officials (8:16–18; 20:23–26) are often read as genuine archival records from David's court, perhaps reworked.
views.L: The chapter repeats the language of the last one: the ram's horn, "each to his tent," the kiss that kills. Joab's two murders, Abner (3:27) and Amasa, mirror each other.
views.J: Rabbinic law used the wise woman's bargain to decide when a town may hand over a person demanded by an enemy. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Terumot 8) Resh Lakish allows it only if, like Sheba, the person is already guilty of death; Rabbi Yochanan says it is enough that he is named. Maimonides allows handing over a named person but says that even then the town is not told to do so at the outset. A midrash names the wise woman Serah daughter of Asher.
views.X: Christian readers have compared Joab's kiss with Judas's (Matthew 26:49), and the one life given for a town with Caiaphas's words about one man dying for the people (John 11:50), while noting the deep difference: Sheba was a rebel; Jesus was innocent.

deep.b:
Joab, son of David's sister Zeruiah, is with David from the beginning to the end. He takes Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 11:6), wins David's wars, carries out the order to put Uriah in the front line (11:14–17), and arranges Absalom's return (14:1–24). He also kills three men on his own authority: Abner (3:27), Absalom (18:14) and Amasa (20:10). David curses him for Abner's death (3:28–29) but never removes him for long.

Readers have read Joab in very different ways. Some see the hard man every king needs, loyal to David's throne even against David's feelings (19:5–7). Others see a killer protecting his own position, whose loyalty ended when he backed Adonijah against Solomon (1 Kings 1:7). David's last instructions leave Joab's fate to Solomon (1 Kings 2:5–6), and Benaiah kills him at the altar (1 Kings 2:28–34).

settings.by: Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite
settings.to: the men of Israel, at Gilgal
settings.when: right after the quarrel with Judah
settings.why: Sheba blows the ram's horn and shouts, "We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse! Everyone to his tents, Israel!" The words were a call for the northern tribes to leave the covenant with David. The same cry was raised when the kingdom split after Solomon (1 Kings 12:16), so readers heard it as a warning.

settings.by: a wise woman of Abel of Beth-maacah
settings.when: while Joab's men batter the walls to capture Sheba
settings.why: She reminds Joab that Abel was famous for settling things by counsel, calls it "a mother in Israel," and asks why he would destroy the LORD's inheritance. Joab says he wants only Sheba. She persuades her town to throw his head over the wall. One wise woman saves a whole town. Readers see wise speech ending the violence that men's swords began.

title: Rizpah's Watch
sum: The last four chapters of 2 Samuel form an appendix, with stories and poems from different parts of David's reign. It opens with a famine that lasts three years. The LORD tells David it is because Saul killed the Gibeonites, a people Israel had sworn by the LORD to protect. The Gibeonites refuse money and ask for seven of Saul's descendants. David spares Jonathan's son Mephibosheth and hands over two sons of Saul's concubine Rizpah and five of his grandsons. They are put to death on the hill at Gibeah at the start of the barley harvest.

Rizpah spreads sackcloth on the rock and guards the bodies from birds and beasts until the rain comes. When David hears of it, he gathers the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead and buries them, with the bones of the seven, in the tomb of Saul's father Kish. "After that, God accepted the prayers made for the land." The chapter ends with four short reports of David's men killing Philistine giants, one of them Goliath of Gath.
readings: Read as a story of a broken oath

God holds Israel to a promise made centuries earlier to a foreign people. Saul's zeal for his own nation does not excuse breaking it. The point is about God's name: a promise sworn by it must be kept.
Read as a story about Rizpah

The kings make the decisions, but a mother's silent watch changes the outcome. God's acceptance of prayer is reported after the burial (21:14), though the rain of 21:10 had already begun to fall. Many modern readers hear the narrator honoring Rizpah's protest.
Read as politics

The famine removes Saul's remaining heirs, which helped David, and David chose which ones died (21:7–8). Critical scholars such as McCarter, Halpern and McKenzie think the story answered charges that David had wiped out Saul's house (16:7–8).

views.H: Traditional readers place the famine early in David's reign, before chapter 9, and accept that Saul attacked the Gibeonites though the attack is not reported in 1 Samuel. The burial at Zela honored Saul's house.
views.C: Critical scholars see chapters 21–24 as an appendix of separate pieces arranged in a ring. Many read 21:1–14 as old tradition that also served David's interests (McCarter); Malamat compared the Hittite king Mursili's plague prayers, which blame a disaster on a broken treaty oath.
views.L: The story turns on silence and action: the Gibeonites speak carefully, the king acts quickly, Rizpah says nothing and keeps watch for months. The phrase that ends it, God accepted prayers for the land, returns at the end of the book (24:25).
views.J: The Talmud says the oath had to be kept because the profaning of God's name was worse than the breach of a single law, and that David then barred the Gibeonites from marrying Israelites (Bavli Yevamot 78b–79a). It explains "Michal" in 21:8 by saying Michal raised her sister Merab's sons (Bavli Sanhedrin 19b).
views.X: Christian readers have struggled with the story. Some read it as a lesson in the seriousness of oaths and corporate guilt; others stress that Scripture forbids children dying for fathers' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16) and that God's acceptance of prayer is reported only after the burial. Rizpah has often been read as a picture of faithful love that refuses to abandon the dead.

deep.b:
The last four chapters are not in time order. Many scholars, from Karl Budde onward, have noticed that they are arranged in a ring:

A. A national disaster caused by a king's sin, ended when God accepts prayer for the land (21:1–14)
B. Heroic deeds of David's warriors (21:15–22)
C. David's song of praise (22)
C. David's last words (23:1–7)
B. Lists and deeds of David's warriors (23:8–39)
A. A national disaster caused by a king's sin, ended when God accepts prayer for the land (24)

The center is poetry: what God has done for David and promised him. The frame is two disasters for which a king is to blame, Saul in the first, David in the second. Walter Brueggemann argued that the appendix deliberately unsettles the heroic picture of David: the king is great, but only by God's help, and his sin costs others dearly.

deep.h: Rizpah and the Gibeonites: three readings
deep.b:
Justice for a broken oath. Israel swore by the LORD to let the Gibeonites live (Joshua 9:15–20). Saul tried to wipe them out. In the Bible's view, bloodguilt not dealt with lies on the land (Numbers 35:33), and a king's house shares in his acts. The narrator has God himself name the cause: "Saul is the reason, Saul and his house of bloodshed" (21:1). On this reading, which many Jewish and Christian interpreters hold, the deaths are the terrible price of God's name being kept holy. The Talmud takes up this very case, including why the bodies could be left hanging despite Deuteronomy 21:23, and says it is better to uproot one letter of the Torah than to let God's name be profaned in public (Bavli Yevamot 78b–79a).

A political purge. Critical historians such as P. Kyle McCarter, Baruch Halpern and Steven McKenzie point out what the story leaves David with: almost no male descendant of Saul except a lame grandson who eats at David's table. Shimei called David "a man of blood" for the blood of Saul's house (16:7–8). And it is David who chooses which of Saul's descendants die (21:7–8). On this reading the oracle and the Gibeonites gave David a religious cover for removing rivals, and the story was told to defend him. The text itself does not say this; it is an inference from who gained.

A theological problem. The law says children must not be put to death for their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16; compare 2 Kings 14:6 and Ezekiel 18). Some readers conclude that the Gibeonites' demand, and David's acceptance, were human choices the narrator records without approving. They notice that God's acceptance of prayer is reported not after the executions but after Rizpah's watch and the burial (21:14). Against this, many commentators (McCarter among them) point out that the rain of 21:10, the sign that the drought was ending, fell while the bodies still hung, so the text may not separate the two so sharply. Others answer that the case was exceptional, an oath sworn in God's name, and that the narrator presents God's answer as real. The chapter leaves the tension for the reader to feel.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the dead who are not numbers
deep.b: This is my own reading. Chapters 21 and 24 both begin with God's anger and end with God accepting prayer for the land. In both, a king treats people as a mass: Saul tries to wipe out a whole people for Israel's sake, David counts his people as soldiers. In both, the turn comes when someone treats the dead or dying as persons: Rizpah guards seven named bodies through a whole season, and David asks, "And these sheep, what did they do?" (24:17). I suggest the appendix is built to make this contrast. The ring structure is widely noted; this particular reading of its two ends is my suggestion.

echoes: Joshua 9:3–27; Numbers 35:31–34; Numbers 25:4; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Deuteronomy 24:16; 1 Samuel 31:8–13; 1 Samuel 18:19; 1 Samuel 17; 1 Chronicles 20:4–8; 16:7–8

settings.what: The famine and the Gibeonites' demand
settings.by: the LORD, then David and the Gibeonites
settings.to: David, then the Gibeonites, then David
settings.when: after three years of famine in David's reign
settings.why: God tells David the famine comes from bloodguilt: Saul broke Israel's oath to the Gibeonites (Joshua 9:15–20) by trying to wipe them out. David asks the Gibeonites how to make atonement. They refuse money and ask for seven of Saul's sons to be executed at Gibeah. The belief behind it was that shed blood pollutes the land until it is answered (Numbers 35:33), and that an oath sworn by the LORD binds Israel for generations. The story is hard to read, and the book does not hide that it removed many of Saul's heirs.
views: Traditional readers see God holding Israel to a promise made to foreigners, and David acting as the law required.
Some scholars note that David's rivals from Saul's line die here, and think Shimei's charge in 16:7–8 may refer to this event. The story then explains why David was not guilty.

settings.what: David's men forbid him to fight
settings.when: after Abishai saves him from the giant Ishbi-benob
settings.why: They swear that he will not go out to battle with them again, "Do not snuff out Israel's lamp." The lamp was a picture of the king's life and the dynasty's future (compare 1 Kings 11:36). The oath shows how much the people's future depended on David's line.

title: The LORD Is My Rock
sum: Near the end of his story David sings a long song of thanks, the same poem found in the book of Psalms as Psalm 18. The LORD is his cliff, fortress, rock and shield. When the waves of death closed over him, he called, and God came down from heaven in storm and fire, rode a cherub on the wind, laid bare the sea bed, and pulled David out of the deep waters.

The second half turns to David's own life: God rewarded his loyalty, trained his hands for battle, gave him sure feet on the heights, and made him head of nations. The song ends with God's loyal love for "his anointed, to David and his line for all time." Placed after the stories of David's sins and sorrows, it reads as the old king's confession that everything he became was God's doing.
readings: Read as David's testimony
The song looks back over a life: the fugitive years under Saul, the wars, the empire. Its pictures come from the wilderness (cliff, stronghold, deer on the heights) and from battle.
Read as a royal psalm

In Psalm 18 the same song was sung in worship. Read there, the speaker is any king of David's line, or the people praying through their king; later Jews and Christians heard the Messiah's voice in it.

views.H: The heading ties the song to David's victories, and many traditional readers take it as written by David after his wars. Its old forms of Hebrew support an early date.
views.C: Cross and Freedman argued that the poem is among the oldest in the Bible, from the 900s BC. Others think it was composed or expanded for the royal temple liturgy. Most agree that 2 Samuel 22 and Psalm 18 are two copies of one poem that drifted apart in transmission.
views.L: The song moves from crisis to rescue to reward to praise. Its storm scene (22:8–16) is one of the great theophanies of the Bible. Placed here, it answers the book's darkest chapters with thanksgiving, and it pairs with Hannah's song at the start of 1 Samuel.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the song as David's thanks for rescue from Saul and all enemies, and its last verse (22:51) is sung at the end of the grace after meals, with "tower" on Sabbaths and festivals and "makes great" on weekdays.
views.X: Paul quotes the song (Romans 15:9) as a prophecy of Gentiles praising God through Christ. Christian readers have heard in the rescue from death a picture of the resurrection, and in the righteous king the one king who fully lived its claims.

deep.b:
The two copies agree in most lines, but they differ in many small places. This table lists the differences that change the wording in English (Samuel first, Psalm second; Psalm verse numbers are the English ones). Smaller differences of spelling and of "and" are left out.

Verse2 Samuel 22Psalm 18
Openingnoneadds "I love you, LORD, my strength" (Psalm 18:1)
22:3"the God of my rock"; ends with "my safe place, my rescuer; from violence you rescue me""my God, my rock" ('eli tsuri); the closing lines are absent (Psalm 18:2)
22:5"breakers of death""Death's ropes" (Psalm 18:4)
22:7"I called"; "my cry for help was in his ears""I cried for help"; "my cry for help came before him, into his ears" (Psalm 18:6)
22:8"the base of the heavens""the base of the mountains" (Psalm 18:7)
22:11"he came into view" (vayyera')"he swooped" (vayyede') (Psalm 18:10)
22:12"shelters"; "massed water" (chashrat)adds "his hiding place" (sitro); "dark water" (cheshkat) (Psalm 18:11)
22:13"fiery coals burst into flame""his clouds swept past, with hail and fiery coals" (Psalm 18:12)
22:14"from the sky" the LORD thundered"in the sky"; adds "hail and fiery coals" again (Psalm 18:13)
22:15"lightning" (baraq)"he shot lightning in plenty" (beraqim rav) (Psalm 18:14)
22:16"the sea's channels"; "when the LORD rebuked""channels of water"; "at your rebuke, LORD" (Psalm 18:15)
22:26"the wholehearted hero" (gibbor)"the wholehearted man" (gevar) (Psalm 18:25)

22:33"God is my fortress of strength"; "he makes my way free" (vayyatter)"the one who wraps me in strength"; "makes my way whole" (vayyitten) (Psalm 18:32)

22:38"I destroyed them""caught them" (Psalm 18:37)
22:39adds "I made an end of them"lacks it (Psalm 18:38)
22:42"they looked""they cried for help" (Psalm 18:41)
22:43"like the ground's dust"; "I crushed them and flattened them""like dust before the wind"; "I emptied them out" (Psalm 18:42)
22:44"my own people's feuds"; "you guarded me""the feuds of the people"; "you made me chief" (Psalm 18:43)
22:45the two lines in one orderthe same two lines in reverse order (Psalm 18:44)
22:46"they come limping""they come trembling" (Psalm 18:45)
22:47"the rock that saves me" (literally "God of the rock of my rescue")"the God who saves me" (Psalm 18:46)
22:48"who lays nations low" (morid)"who brings nations down" (vayyadber) (Psalm 18:47)
22:49"who leads me out" (motsi'i)"who frees me" (mefalleti) (Psalm 18:48)

Most differences are the kind that arise when a text is copied by hand for centuries: letters that look alike (d and r, kh and r), dropped or added letters, spelling updated in one copy and not the other. Some look like deliberate changes for worship, such as the Psalm's opening line. Scholars disagree about which copy is older overall; most think each has the better reading in some places (Cross and Freedman).

The books of Samuel open and close with a song. Hannah's (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and David's share key words: God as a rock with no equal (1 Samuel 2:2; 22:32), the horn lifted high (1 Samuel 2:1, 2:10; 22:3), Sheol and rescue from death (1 Samuel 2:6; 22:6), thunder from heaven (1 Samuel 2:10; 22:14), the humble raised and the proud brought low (1 Samuel 2:7–8; 22:28), and God's king and anointed (1 Samuel 2:10; 22:51). Hannah sang of a king before Israel had one; David, the king, sings back her themes. Many scholars, such as Brevard Childs and Robert Polzin, have argued that the two songs were placed to frame the whole story of the rise of kingship.

echoes: Psalm 18; 1 Samuel 2:1–10; Exodus 15:1–18; Deuteronomy 32; Habakkuk 3:19; Proverbs 30:5; Romans 15:9; Luke 1:69; 7:12–16

settings.to: the LORD; no other hearers are named
settings.when: according to its heading, on the day the LORD rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul
settings.why: David praises God as his rock, fortress and shield. He describes God coming down in storm and fire to pull him out of deep waters, and he claims that God rewarded him for his clean hands. It ends with God's loyal love to "his anointed, to David and his line for all time." Placed near the end of the book, after David's sins, it reminds readers that his story was finally one of God's faithfulness. The same song appears as Psalm 18, so it was also sung in Israel's worship.
views: Traditional readers take the heading at its word, and many critical scholars agree the poem is very old, perhaps from the 10th century BC, because of its early language.
A royal psalm for the king's line
Others think it was sung for later kings of David's line at festivals, and that its last line was meant for them.

Many scholars note that chapters 21–24 form a ring, with this song and David's last words at the center. Walter Brueggemann argued that the frame of famine, plague and royal failure around the songs undercuts the royal claims built up in chapters 5–8. Others read the songs at the center as the book's last word of praise.

title: Last Words and Mighty Men
sum: David's "last words" are a short poem in the style of a prophet's oracle. The LORD's Spirit speaks through him: a king who rules with justice and reverence for God is like sunrise after rain, bringing grass out of the ground. God has made an everlasting covenant with David's house. The worthless, by contrast, are thorns fit only for burning.

Then comes the roll of David's warriors: the Three, whose exploits are told in brief, bold stories (eight hundred slain at once, a hand frozen to a sword, a field of lentils held alone); the three who broke through the Philistine lines to bring David water from Bethlehem, which he poured out to the LORD; Abishai and Benaiah, who outranked the Thirty (Benaiah killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day); and the Thirty, ending with the name of Uriah the Hittite.
readings: Read as the ideal and the reality
The poem describes the king God wants; the list remembers the men who made David's kingdom. Its last name, Uriah, is a reminder of how far David fell from the ideal.
Read as a messianic oracle
The Targum, and many Jewish and Christian readers after it, heard in the just ruler of 23:3–4 the coming Messiah, whose rule is like morning light.

views.H: The list of the Thirty is widely accepted, even by many critical scholars, as an old record from David's time. Several names (Asahel, Uriah, Eliam) tie it to stories elsewhere in Samuel.
views.C: Scholars debate the date of the poem in 23:1–7; some think it old, others a later composition in David's name. The list of heroes is thought to have grown over time (Elliger); Mazar saw in the Thirty an official body of David's elite officers.
views.L: The list reads like a heroic saga, with short exploit stories in a set pattern. The narrator credits each victory to the LORD (23:10, 23:12) and ends with the name that recalls chapter 11.
views.J: The Targum reads the oracle of the just ruler as speaking of the Messiah. The Talmud reads the water story as a legal question about using others' property to save oneself (Bavli Bava Kamma 60b), and connects Eliam son of Ahithophel with Bathsheba's family (Bavli Sanhedrin 69b).
views.X: The New Testament calls David a prophet who spoke by the Spirit (Acts 2:30; Mark 12:36), and Christians read the everlasting covenant (23:5) as fulfilled in Jesus. David's pouring out of the water has often been preached as a picture of costly devotion.

deep.h: The heroes in Samuel and in Chronicles
deep.b:
1 Chronicles 11:10–47 gives the same list, with many differences. Some examples: the first hero is "Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite" in Samuel, "Jashobeam son of Hachmoni" in Chronicles, and he kills eight hundred in Samuel, three hundred in Chronicles. Chronicles names the place of Eleazar's stand, Pas-dammim, and combines it with the field story that Samuel gives to Shammah; the field holds barley, not lentils. Samuel's "Mebunnai the Hushathite" is "Sibbecai" in Chronicles, "Heleb" is "Heled," "Hiddai" is "Hurai," "Abi-albon" is "Abiel," and "Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite" appears to be "Ahijah the Pelonite." After Uriah, Chronicles adds sixteen more names, many from east of the Jordan.

Most of the name differences are copying errors in one list or the other; letters such as b and k, or d and r, are easily confused. Chronicles probably used a text of Samuel that differed from ours, and it may have used a longer source list as well. Neither list is free of damage, and scholars correct each by the other.

deep.title: Claude's theory: water that cost blood
deep.b: This is my own reading. In 23:15–17 David refuses to drink water his men risked their lives for. He calls it "the blood of the men" and pours it out to the LORD. The list then ends with Uriah (23:39), one of these same warriors, whose life David spent to hide his own sin (11:14–17). I suggest the narrator placed the water story and the list's last name to make the reader feel the contrast: the David who honored his men's blood at Adullam and the David who shed Uriah's at Rabbah. Commentators have noted the pointed ending with Uriah; I have not seen this link to the water story made explicitly, though it may have been.

settings.by: David, speaking as a prophet by the LORD's Spirit
settings.to: no hearers are named; it is called "the declaration of David son of Jesse"
settings.when: near the end of his life
settings.why: David says the Spirit spoke through him: a king who rules justly and in fear of God is like morning sunlight after rain, which makes grass grow. He trusts that God has made "a covenant with me that lasts forever," and that the worthless will be burned like thorns. It sets the standard for every later king from David's line, who were probably meant to hear it. Readers in hard times heard it as a promise of a just king to come (compare Isaiah 11:1–5).
views: Traditional readers take it as David's final prophecy.
Many critical scholars think it is an early poem about the ideal king, attributed to David, with the line about the everlasting covenant echoing chapter 7.

settings.to: his men in the stronghold, and then the LORD
settings.when: at harvest, when a Philistine post holds Bethlehem
settings.why: David longs aloud for water from Bethlehem's well, and three warriors break through the Philistine camp to bring it. David will not drink it. He pours it out to the LORD, saying it is the blood of men who risked their lives. The act honors his men and gives God what cost them so much. It shows the bond between David and his warriors.

title: The Price of a Threshing Floor
sum: The LORD's anger burns against Israel again, and he stirs David up to count Israel and Judah. Joab protests but is overruled. For nearly ten months the army officers travel the land, east of the Jordan, north to Dan and Sidon, south to Beersheba. The count: 800,000 fighting men in Israel, 500,000 in Judah. Then David's heart strikes him, and he confesses that he has sinned and acted like a fool.

The prophet Gad brings him a choice: seven years of famine, three months of flight before his enemies, or three days of pestilence. David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand. Seventy thousand die. As the angel reaches toward Jerusalem, the LORD says, "That's enough!" David asks that the punishment fall on him and his family instead of the sheep. At Gad's word he buys the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, refuses to offer the LORD what costs him nothing, builds an altar, and the plague stops. The place will later be the site of the temple.
readings: Read as a story of sin and grace
The king sins by trusting in numbers; he confesses, intercedes for his people, and pays full price for a place of sacrifice. The book ends not with David's greatness but with God's mercy.
Read as the founding of the temple site

Chronicles makes it explicit that Araunah's threshing floor became the temple's site (1 Chronicles 22:1; 2 Chronicles 3:1). Samuel's last story explains why that hill is holy: there God stopped his angel.
Read alongside Chronicles

1 Chronicles 21 tells the same story with differences: Satan stirs David, the numbers differ, and David pays six hundred shekels of gold. Comparing the two shows how a later writer reread an earlier text.

views.H: Traditional readers take the census and plague as real events late in David's reign. The circuit of the census traces the actual borders of David's kingdom, and the threshing floor on the hill north of the City of David is the later temple mount.
views.C: Critical scholars see an old story explaining the origin of the Jerusalem altar, placed as the book's last word. Many think Chronicles' substitution of Satan reflects a later theology. The census numbers are widely judged far too large for the 900s BC.
views.L: The chapter mirrors chapter 21 and ends with the same words. David, who began as a shepherd (1 Samuel 16:11), ends as a shepherd pleading for his sheep. Joab, the hard man, is the voice of caution.
views.J: Rashi, following Midrash Tehillim, explains David's choice: in famine those with grain stores survive, and choosing the sword would look like trusting his warriors, but in a plague all are equal. On the census, Josephus says David forgot the half-shekel that Moses required at every count; the Talmud says Israel may not be counted head by head (Bavli Yoma 22b) and that God let David stumble over the half-shekel rule because he had called God an "inciter" (Bavli Berakhot 62b); Ramban says a count without need or command is wrong. Rabbinic tradition identifies the threshing floor with Mount Moriah, where Isaac was bound.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in David's plea a picture of the good shepherd who offers himself for the sheep (John 10:11), and in the altar on Araunah's floor, the future temple site, a step toward the place where God would meet his people. The tension between 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1 has been read through Job 1–2 and James 1:13.

deep.h: Who stirred David up? 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1
deep.b:
Samuel says, "The LORD's anger burned against Israel once more. He stirred David up against them" (24:1). Chronicles, written after the exile, retells it: "Satan stood up against Israel and stirred David up to count Israel" (1 Chronicles 21:1). The verb is the same.

Both are true. A common reading, especially among Christian interpreters, says God permitted or used an adversary to do what God intended as judgment, as in Job 1–2, where the satan acts only with God's leave, and 1 Kings 22:19–23, where a spirit goes out from God's court to deceive Ahab. On this view Samuel names the ultimate cause and Chronicles the immediate one.

An adversary, not Satan. In Chronicles satan has no article, so it may mean "an adversary," as in 19:22 and 1 Kings 11:14. Sara Japhet suggests the Chronicler meant a human enemy whose threat drove David to count his troops, or left the figure deliberately vague. Peggy Day argues more broadly that satan in the Hebrew Bible is a common noun for various adversaries, human or heavenly, and that no single figure "Satan" appears in it.

A development in Israel's thought. Many critical scholars trace how "the satan" grew from an ordinary word for an opponent to a heavenly accuser (Job; Zechariah 3) and finally, in later Jewish and Christian writings, the devil. On this view the Chronicler could no longer say plainly that God incited a sin.

God's sovereignty and human guilt. Some theologians, especially in the Reformed tradition, take Samuel at its word: God rules even over sinful choices without being their author, and David is still guilty (24:10). James 1:13, that God tempts no one, is often cited on the other side. The two texts together keep both God's rule and human responsibility in view.

A rabbinic answer. The Talmud links the verb to David's own words to Saul, that if the LORD had "incited" Saul against him, an offering would appease God (1 Samuel 26:19). Because David called God an inciter, God let him stumble over a rule schoolchildren know, the half-shekel paid at a census (Exodus 30:12; Bavli Berakhot 62b). Rashi, on why God was angry in the first place, says simply that he does not know.

The Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a, copied about 50–25 BC, preserves fragments of 2 Samuel 24. As reported in published studies, it agrees with Chronicles against the Masoretic Text at important points: it seems to have had the scene of David seeing the angel with drawn sword over Jerusalem and the elders "covered in sackcloth" (after 24:16; compare 1 Chronicles 21:16), it reportedly reads "I the shepherd did wrong" with the Greek (24:17), and it seems to mention Arna (Araunah) threshing wheat and the king's servants coming "covered in sackcloth" (24:20; compare 1 Chronicles 21:20). Only parts of these lines survive, and much of the wording is restored from Chronicles. Frank Moore Cross (2006) proposed a new reconstruction of 24:16–22, and Innocent Himbaza (2010) re-examined what can actually be read and cautioned against relying on the restorations, in scholarship and in Bible translations.

Most scholars (Ulrich, McKenzie and others) conclude from these readings that the Chronicler worked from a Hebrew text of Samuel like the scroll's, not from the Masoretic form, and that some of Chronicles' "additions" were in his source. Others think the scroll and Chronicles were shaped by each other's kind of text, or that the evidence in these broken lines is too thin to carry that conclusion here, whatever is true elsewhere in Samuel.

The Greek has its own differences: three years of famine instead of seven (24:13), the plague ending "at the hour of the midday meal" (24:15, Greek), and a final sentence about Solomon enlarging the altar (24:25). All of 2 Samuel 19–24 lies inside the kaige section (2 Samuel 11:2 to 1 Kings 2:11), where Codex Vaticanus, and so Rahlfs' edition, carries a text revised toward the Hebrew. The Lucianic (Antiochene) manuscripts are the better witness to the Old Greek here. The three Greek readings just named are reported in both, which makes them likely Old Greek; the Lucianic text also has readings of its own, such as "they began from Aroer" (24:5) and "Joab and the commanders" (24:2).

What this rests on: the reports of 4QSam-a here come from Ulrich's The Qumran Text of Samuel and Josephus (1978), McCarter's commentary (1984), Cross (2006), Himbaza (2010), Tov's textbook, and the translation in The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible, which marks the 24:20 reconstruction as speculative. I could not consult the official edition (DJD 17, 2005) directly, so the exact preserved letters should be checked there. The variants on 24:16, 24:17 and 24:20 give each reading.

Samuel counts 800,000 men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah, 1,300,000 fighting men. Chronicles counts 1,100,000 and 470,000, without Levi and Benjamin. Josephus gives a third pair, 900,000 and 400,000 (Antiquities 7.320). With women, children and the old, either figure implies a population of four or five million, which most archaeologists think far beyond what the hill country could support in the 900s BC. Answers include copying errors in numbers, different groups counted, and reading 'elef as "unit" or "clan" instead of "thousand." The census topic gives the views at length.

echoes: 1 Chronicles 21:1–22:1; 2 Chronicles 3:1; Exodus 30:11–16; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 23:3–16; 21:1; 21:14; 1 Samuel 24:5; Job 1:6–12; James 1:13; John 10:11; Sirach 2:18

settings.what: The order to count the people
settings.by: the LORD stirs David; David orders Joab
settings.when: when the LORD's anger burns against Israel again
settings.why: David orders a census of fighting men from Dan to Beersheba. Joab objects, but the king wins. A census was a way to measure military power and to tax, and Israel was to be counted only with a ransom paid to the LORD (Exodus 30:12). The order is presented as a sin that brings a plague. Here the LORD stirs David up; 1 Chronicles 21:1 says it was "Satan" (the Hebrew word means "adversary"). Readers have long asked how the two fit.
views: Some readers think the text means God used David's own pride to judge Israel for some earlier sin.
Many scholars think Chronicles changed the cause to an adversary so that God would not seem to cause the sin he punished.

settings.what: David's confession and Gad's three choices
settings.when: after the count is finished, nine months and twenty days later
settings.why: David admits he has sinned and been a fool. Gad brings God's offer of three punishments: famine, flight from enemies, or plague. David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand, "for his compassion runs deep." Readers see a king who knows God's mercy is greater than human mercy, even when he is being punished.

settings.when: when he sees the angel striking the people
settings.why: David says, "It is I who sinned," and asks God to punish him and his family, not "these sheep." The shepherd king offers himself for his flock. It is the book's last picture of David's heart.

settings.what: The altar on Araunah's threshing floor
settings.by: Gad the prophet, then David and Araunah the Jebusite
settings.when: the same day, as the plague reaches Jerusalem
settings.why: Gad tells David to build an altar on Araunah's threshing floor. Araunah offers it free, but David refuses: "I will not offer the LORD my God burnt offerings I got for free." He pays and sacrifices, and the plague stops. Later tradition identified this place as the site of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 3:1). Readers who worshiped there learned its holy ground was bought by a king's repentance.
